newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba heralds EMU with 2-yr policy strategy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba heralds EMU with 2-yr policy strategy.

text.p: The German Bundesbank on Thursday paved the way for the start of European monetary union, mapping out the basis for its policy until the European Central Bank takes the monetary reins at the end of 1998.

The central bank left interest rates unchanged after its last policy-making meeting of the year, but set a slightly more restrictive target for growth in its main monetary policy indicator, M3 money supply.

The central bank left the discount rate at 2.50 percent and the Lombard emergency financing rate at 4.50 percent. It kept the main money market rate, the repo, steady at three percent for the next three weeks. It has held this level since August.

In a move aimed at smoothing the transition to Europe's single currency, the central bank said it would extend its money supply orientation to a two-year period, so bridging a possible period of market uncertainty in 1998.

During that year, currencies which will enter monetary union will be irrevocably fixed against each other, forcing those central banks affected to coordinate policy very closely until the ECB takes over policy at the start of 1999.
"The two year orientation is aimed at making the start-up for the European Central Bank as frictionless as possible," Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer told a news conference.
The central bank set a growth target of between 3.5 percent and 6.5 percent for the M3 money supply measure in 1997, slightly lower than the current 4-7 percent range.
It added in a statement that M3 growth of about five percent in 1997 and 1998 would be appropriate.

Economists polled by Reuters expected no change in interest rates but had been divided over whether the M3 target would be kept unchanged at four to seven percent or whether it would be lowered slightly.

The Bundesbank traditionally compiles its M3 target by looking at likely developments in growth and prices, making adjustments for changes in the way in which money is being used, and then placing a target corridor around its central estimate of M3 growth needs.

For 1997, it used an assessment of production potential at just over two percent, unavoidable inflation of between 1.5 and two percent and a one percent element to compensate for slower velocity of circulation of money.
Velocity of circulation is a measure of how intensively funds are used in the economy.

Tietmeyer told a news conference that the two-year M3 money supply growth target was meant to head off any volatility on financial markets that could be disturbed in 1998 in the run-up to a single European currency.
"This is a clear signal of stability for the markets," he said, adding that the M3 money supply measure remained the best indicator for monetary policy.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel welcomed the Bundesbank's decision to tighten its target for M3 money growth and to extend the period it covered to two years as a good basis for Europe's single currency.

"With this decision the German Bundesbank underlines its commitment to making a contribution towards creating a stable European currency in a united Europe," Waigel said in a statement released in Bonn.

Tietmeyer welcomed the decision by European Union leaders earlier this month to adopt a "stability pact" to ensure budgetary discipline after monetary union begins, but said this was something central banks would have little influence over.
"(That) is a clear political decision. Overall I think in Dublin the central significance of clear budgetary discipline was recognised," he said.

The important thing was that EU leaders had agreed to limit budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product as outlined in the Maastricht Treaty, he said, adding that the success of the stability pact would depend on the level of self-commitment of EU member states.
